claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature plastic strain than commercially used pure tungsten.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature toughness than commercially used pure tungsten.
The multicomponent chemistry of WTaTiVZr induces a refined dual-phase microstructure.
The multicomponent chemistry of WTaTiVZr produces nanoscale precipitates.
Ta, Ti, V, and Zr alter or segregate to grain boundaries in WTaTiVZr.
Nanoscale precipitates and altered grain boundaries inhibit dislocation pile-up.
Nanoscale precipitates and altered grain boundaries impede crack propagation.
Refractory alloying elements in WTaTiVZr trigger nucleation of finely dispersed precipitates.
Interrupting dislocation pile-up increases effective dislocation mobility in WTaTiVZr.
The proposed microstructural refinement delays crack initiation.
Delayed crack initiation and propagation increase the plastic strain and toughness of WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten.
Under identical testing at 1200–1400 °C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit more plastic deformation than pure tungsten.
Under identical testing at 1200–1400 °C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater fracture toughness than pure tungsten.
W tested after deformation will show a higher dislocation density near precipitates and modified grain boundaries than pure tungsten.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply approximately from 1200 to 1400 °C under plasma-facing operating conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at low temperatures or under irradiation conditions more extreme than those tested.
The individual contributions of W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr to the proposed microstructural changes have not been quantified.
Precipitate toughening may compete with precipitate-induced embrittlement in WTaTiVZr.
The comparison will use equimolar WTaTiVZr and high-purity tungsten prepared under nominally identical processing and test conditions.
